articles.title_zh: Nike stock sinks as revenue misses estimates
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
What happened: Nike ( NKE ) stock fell as much as 6% in after-hours trading on Thursday.
What's behind the move: Nike posted fiscal first quarter revenue of $11.21 billion, versus consensus estimates of $11.33 billion.
Earnings per share came in at $0.48, down from $0.49 a year ago.
The company said revenues are expected to decline in the high single digits in fiscal 2027. Nike's gross margin, however, expanded 60 basis points to 42.8%.
The results come nearly two years after Elliott Hill took the helm as CEO.
"This is a quarter you'd expect from a new CEO three or four quarters in, but not two years in," CFRA analyst Zach Warring, who has a Buy on the stock, told Yahoo Finance.
The analyst noted, "valuations and expectations have been reset."
"Now they can kind of move forward and begin to return to growth, expand margins and start to really work on some of the geographies that they're sluggish, which is obviously greater China and Europe," he added.
Read more: Caitlin Clark's new signature Nike shoe nearly sells out within first two hours of going on sale
What else you need to know: The company was already facing challenges when Hill took over. Nike had pulled back from several major retail partners as it sought to prioritize its own sales channels, giving competitors an opening to gain ground.
The turnaround has not been easy.
"We have more work to do in NIKE Sportswear, Jordan Brand and Greater China, and we're taking deliberate actions to strengthen those businesses the right way for the long-term," Hill said in the company's earnings release.
In late August, Dick's Sporting Goods ( DKS ) offered up a brutal warning about its business, in part because Nike is heavily discounting slow-moving product.
Soccer icon Kylian Mbappé ended his long-term business tie-up with Nike last month and announced he will now be joining Swiss sports giant On ( ONON ).
Nike's stock recently dropped from the S&P 100 ( ^SP100 ) after nearly 20 years in the index.
Thursday's report is the first earnings release under new CFO Dave Denton, who previously held a role at Pfizer.
Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance.

"A number of properties are currently being evacuated in the Whelford area following the declaration of a major incident," Gloucestershire Police said in a statement. "It follows the arrest of several men on suspicion of offenses under the explosives act."

articles.title_zh: Top Democratic appropriator wants White House to pay for airing ‘propaganda’
articles.content_orig:
The National Capital Planning Commission on Thursday unanimously voted to approve building plans for a new White House Visitor Screening Facility.
The project is part of President Donald Trump’s massive overhaul of the White House grounds, but one that has enjoyed bipartisan support and drawn little pushback compared to his other construction plans.
The facility will be built off 15th Street in Sherman Park, with an entrance that leads below ground for screening and allows visitors to exit by the East Wing of the White House, the site of the president’s more controversial ballroom project.
The commission’s chairman, Trump appointee Mark Paoletta, said Thursday, “I look forward to the beautiful building be built on the White House grounds.”
Lee Webb, an urban planner with the 12-member commission, presented the final plans for the facility. He said it will include a versatile indoor open-floor-plan space that will allow the Secret Service to install permanent screening technology. The space will also allow significant indoor queuing for large events, with a 700-person occupancy within the screening facility.
Visitors to the White House are now screened in temporary, double-wide trailers and tents, which the Secret Service has said falls short of its security needs.
The plans were approved by all members of the commission, which includes representatives appointed by Washington Mayor Muriel Bowser, a Democrat.
Construction work is expected to begin in the next month and finish at some point in 2028.
Representing the General Services Administration on the board, Trump appointee Paul Ingrassia hailed the addition of the new facility as “an incredible part of this White House reimagining we’ve been seeing.”
That includes the massive 90,000-square-foot ballroom that’s being constructed at the site of the former East Wing. The commission approved the plans for the ballroom in April.
At Thursday’s hearing, one of the presenters said the exit of the new facility will have Corinthian columns to “align with the ballroom’s language.”
The president has been highly involved in renovations at the White House, which have included gold adornments in the Oval Office and the installation of a helipad on the White House lawn, as well as other projects around D.C., like the proposed construction of a “ Triumphal Arch .”
Dareh Gregorian is a politics reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: What happened in the failed execution of Christa Pike - and what next?
articles.title_zh: What happened in the failed execution of Christa Pike - and what next?
articles.content_orig:
What we know after Christa Pike survived two lethal injections
US convicted murderer Christa Pike is in a critical condition in hospital after Tennessee authorities failed to execute her by lethal injection, her lawyer says.
The case of Pike, whose attempted execution on Wednesday had already been the subject of a high-profile legal battle, has raised a number of questions.
These include what went wrong, what happens next, and - for opponents of the death penalty - fresh concerns around the suffering of an inmate when an execution does not go to plan.
A review into what happened has been ordered and executions in Tennessee have been halted for the rest of the year, Governor Bill Lee said.
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, an attack that carried out alongside her then-boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp, who was 17. Shipp remains in prison, having been spared the death penalty under state law.
Pike was scheduled to be put to death in Tennessee on Wednesday evening local time. The injections were allowed by the Supreme Court at the eleventh hour after the legal battle.
Pike was given two injections of the drug pentobarbital but her legal team said these failed to stop her heartbeat and that she could still be heard snoring.
Watch: Witnesses recount Christa Pike's failed execution attempt
Tennessee halts executions after death row inmate Christa Pike survives hers
US death row inmate survives execution attempt after two lethal injections
The Tennessee Department of Correction has defended the method it used, saying "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out."
The state protocol does not clearly specify what should happen if an inmate remains alive after a second dose, according to the AP news agency.
Authorities are yet to say whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have yet to give their explanation of why the dosage given to Pike was non-fatal, although medical experts have given theories.
Dr Joel Zivot, a professor at the Emory University School of Medicine, told the BBC Pike probably never achieved a sufficient blood level of pentobarbital to cause her breath to stop or heart failure.
The Tennessee correction department said Pike had been taken to an off-site medical facility, while one of her lawyers said on Wednesday that she was being given "life-saving measures" in hospital.
On Thursday, lawyer Randy Spivey told reporters: "We don't have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment."
He added: "But we do know that that she is alive right now."
In his emailed comments to the BBC, Zivot said: "It's very possible that as a consequence of the delay of the beginning of resuscitation she will have a brain injury."
A third-party review has been ordered by state Governor Bill Lee, who said on Thursday that Tennessee will halt executions for the rest of the year.
This could impact any additional attempt by the state to execute Pike in the near-term, if she does regain consciousness.
May Martinez, the mother of Colleen Slemmer who had pushed for Pike's execution to take place, told NBC News the events had been "a mess".
Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed by Pike and her boyfriend
Historically, the US Supreme Court has not halted second attempts at executions, said John Mills, a lawyer who works with inmates sentenced to death.
In 2024, it allowed Alabama to proceed with a second execution of Kenneth Eugene Smith, used an experimental oxygen deprivation method, after their attempt to kill him by lethal injection failed two years before.
A notable Supreme Court case from 1947 allowed the state of Louisiana to try a second electrocution of Willie Smith, a black teenager whose first execution attempt failed when he was 17 years old.
The court found a second execution would not violate the Constitution's prohibitions against double jeopardy or cruel and unusual punishment and Smith was executed aged 18.
"If the question is, is it likely the federal courts would intervene in a second attempt? I'm afraid the answer is a resounding no," Mills said of Pike's case.
Pike's lawyers have already filed a motion to stay her execution.
Mills said that if he was her lawyer, he would be asking both the federal courts and Tennessee court to reconsider their views on a second attempt and would also approach Governor Lee, who has powers to issue stays of executions and exercise clemency.
Opponents of the death penalty have been quick to react.
Maya Foa, the head of international legal organisation Reprieve, said: "We cannot know exactly what went wrong, because so much happened behind a curtain â lethal injection relies on secrecy at every stage, to hide the violence of the state taking a human life."
Pentobarbital is a potent sedative that slows down the body, including the nervous system. Doctors sometimes use it as a treatment for certain conditions but in high doses it can also be used as a lethal injection to cause death.
Its use in lethal injections came under renewed scrutiny last year after a US federal government review during the Biden administration raised concerns about the drug's potential for "unnecessary pain and suffering".
The Biden government banned its use in federal executions but that did not bind individual states such as Tennessee, which can choose their own methods.
Why the death penalty is on the rise in US
In recent years, states have found some drugs needed for lethal injections harder to come by, because pharmaceutical companies have opposed the use of their products for such purposes.
Some manufacturers have explicitly said they will no longer produce pentobarbital or will restrict their use in executions, according to Alexis Hoag-Fordjor, Co-Director of the Center for Criminal Justice at Brooklyn Law School.
In 2024, for instance, the manufacturer Absolute Standards said it would no longer make the drug. , external
The Tennessee correction department has not specifically addressed an allegation from Pike's legal team that the pentobarbital it used was "degraded". Drugs may degrade for a number of reasons, including if it has aged beyond its use-by date and its potency has decreased.
But the department issued a broader defence of its method, writing in a statement: "The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective."
"It's unclear, the quality and the effectiveness of the drug" used in Pike's execution, Hoag-Fordjor told the BBC, given how difficult it has been for states like Tennessee to obtain pentobarbital.
"It shouldn't be a surprise something went wrong," he said.
The predicament Tennessee authorities found themselves in - having to call emergency medical services to save Pike after trying to kill her - suggested there was "no plan in place" for a scenario like Pike's, Hoag-Fordjor added.
The attempted execution of Pike was not the first in Tennessee in 2026 that did not go to plan.
The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein to administer a lethal injection. He was given a one-year reprieve by Governor Bill Lee.
More widely across the US, the issue of botched executions continues to cause alarm.
In 2022, more than a third of executions in the US were botched or highly problematic, according to the Death Penalty Information Center (DPI) - an organisation that provides statistics and research on the death penalty but does not take a stance on it morally.

In 204, the execution of Clayton Lockett was postponed after 20 minutes because a lethal injection of three drugs failed to work properly when one of his veins ruptured and he went on to writhe and shake uncontrollably.

Fears that US deficit is unsustainable also drive UK 30-year bond yields briefly above 6% for first time since 1998
Business live – latest updates
The global bond sell-off intensified on Thursday, driving 10-year US government borrowing costs to their highest level in 24 years in a frantic day’s trading.
The threat of a renewed round of inflation from the persistently high cost of oil has spooked investors on both sides of the Atlantic, with central banks expected to raise interest rates in the coming months to prevent price increases from becoming embedded.
The sell-off drove the yield, or interest rate, on 10-year US Treasuries to 5.34% – the highest level since 2002.
In the UK, where surging borrowing costs are increasing the pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, before his first budget later this month, the yield on 30-year bonds hit 6% for the first time since 1998, before easing slightly later in the day. Yields on five- and 10-year UK bonds were also up.
Stock market investors sold heavily too, knocking almost 1.7% off the FTSE 100 in London – its worst daily fall since May. Bourses in other parts of Europe were also hit, with Germany’s DAX falling 1% and France’s CAC 40 losing 1.6%.
“There is carnage in the bond market, which is hitting stocks hard,” said Neil Wilson, the investor strategist at Saxo UK. “It looks like the relentless rout in the bond market is sending investors running for cover.”
The bond sell-off around the world is being driven by fears of high inflation, as the Middle East conflict continues to restrict oil supplies from the region.
Japan’s 10-year yield rose towards the 30-year high set last month.
US bonds weakened despite inflation data on Wednesday coming in lower than forecast, which was expected to calm investors’ nerves about the prospect of further increases in the cost of borrowing by the US Federal Reserve.
Traders remain anxious that the Fed will continue to raise interest rates to fight inflation, mainly in response to the strength of the US economy and the prospect of workers bidding up their wages.
Mohit Kumar, an economist at Jefferies, said there was growing concern at the amount of debt being issued to fund government deficits, as well as inflation concerns.
“Inflation, deficit and issuance concerns continue to weigh on the bond market,” he said.
“There is also a buyers’ strike as investors do not want to step in till we get some form of stability. Hedge funds have suffered in the latest round of sell-off and do not have the risk appetite to fade the move. Real money potentially has the risk appetite, but won’t step in till we get some stability.”

Axel Rudolph, the chief technical analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “While the latest data has reduced expectations of an October Fed rate hike, investors remain wary that persistent inflation and higher oil prices could keep rates elevated for longer.
“The dollar is benefiting from that caution, climbing to a three-month high, while the prospect of a December rate increase keeps pressure on bond markets.”
Oil prices rose again on Thursday, despite analysis that showed exports of crude from the strait of Hormuz have largely returned to levels seen before the outbreak of the Iran war , as oil producers and the shipping industry have found alternative ways of transporting crucial fuel out of the Middle East.
Brent crude rose 3% to about $101 a barrel.
The price of crude remained at elevated levels as traders balanced the recovery in some Middle East exports with uncertainty over a long-term solution to the conflict and reopening of the strait.
Eurozone countries were also caught up in the wave of selling, with France in particular in investors’ sights. Ten-year yields on French government bonds hit 4.96%, the highest level since 2002.
The spread over German yields – an indicator of the additional risk France is believed to face – has jumped to its highest level in more than a decade.

A judge in Washington, D.C., has thrown out a criminal case against a former Olympian accused of damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool — and blocked prosecutors from trying to charge him again.
U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro had already agreed to drop felony charges against 67-year-old David Hearn after she admitted that the damage was likely caused by “botched” construction. But she wanted to leave open the possibility of prosecuting Hearn again after Donald Trump’s demands.
On Thursday, the judge called that idea “simply fanciful” and permanently tossed the case.
Hearn “faces the unique possibility that the government will revive this case, one that it has already announced to be meritless — based on political pressure brought by the President of the United States upon his subordinate officers,” DC Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman wrote Thursday.
“The Court respects the authority of the Office of the United States Attorney to decide which cases to prosecute and which to dismiss,” Edelman wrote. “However, in the exceptional circumstances posed by this case, the government has no right to retain the ability to compound the errors it has already made, or even to threaten to do so, at Mr. Hearn’s expense.”
The dismissal of the case with prejudice ensures that the Department of Justice “cannot bring this case against him again,” Hearn’s lawyers said in a statement shared with The Independent.
“This decision is a victory for the rule of law and for an innocent American seeking justice,” attorneys Norm Eisen with the Democracy Defenders Fund, Mary Dohrmann of Washington Litigation Group and Steve Levin and Michael Bromwich of Steptoe LLP said in a joint statement.
“This case never should have been brought in the first place,” they added. “This was a miscarriage of justice, and what happened to Mr. Hearn is an outrage that should shock every American.”
The decision marks the likely end of a months-long legal battle after prosecutors accused Hearn of tearing out the recently applied “American flag blue” liner that started to flap to the surface shortly after it was installed earlier this year.
Weeks after she publicly accused Hearn of “forcefully and violently” ripping out the liner, Pirro’s office admitted that the sealant started to peel “almost immediately” after the work was completed.
Contractors left behind “widespread damage,” prosecutors wrote in court filings.
It was not until after the indictment was filed that the Department of Interior determined that the “damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism,” they wrote.
Trump, however, has demanded that Pirro re-open the case while accusing her of having “folded like an umbrella” and “choking.”
On Truth Social, Trump called Hearn’s attorney Norm Eisen a “Political Hack” and “TRUMP DERANGED SLEAZEBAG” as he pushed Pirro to “re-visit her hastily made decision” to drop the case.
Hearn — a champion canoeist who represented the U.S. at the 1992, 1996, and 2000 Summer Olympics — argued that Trump’s comments suggest the administration is trying to charge him again as part of a politically motivated attack.
Edelman hauled lawyers to court last month to hear why prosecutors would want to keep the door open to re-charging Hearn despite admitting there isn’t any evidence to do so.
The Trump administration, meanwhile, continues to funnel millions of taxpayer dollars into renovating the Reflecting Pool , bringing total costs for the project to nearly $20 million.
In July, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said the Trump administration would not seek any new contracts after costs exploded to more than $17 million.
But federal spending records show that the National Park Service awarded a nearly $2.7 million contract last month to American Ag Energy Inc., for the maintenance, repair and rebuilding of water purification and sewage treatment equipment.
The president initially said a refurbishing project for the iconic 2,030-foot pool could be done quickly for $1.5 million in time for White House-backed Fourth of July celebrations in the nation’s capital.
But those costs quickly surged to nearly $7 million after an initial no-bid contract was handed to a Virginia-based firm. That company, Atlantic Industrial Coatings LLC, was awarded another $6.2 million in May. On June 3, the company received another $1 million, followed by more than $461,000 on June 15.
The shallow pool, which the president repeatedly promotes as “bigger than skyscrapers,” was refurbished with a shade of dark blue and outfitted with “advanced nanobubbler technology” to tackle algae blooms that have long plagued the landmark.
But shortly after workers refilled the pool, the algae returned, and the recently applied sealant in the Trump-requested blue hue started to peel and float to the surface.

Fears that US deficit is unsustainable also drive UK 30-year bond yields briefly above 6% for first time since 1998
Business live – latest updates
The global bond sell-off intensified on Thursday, driving 10-year US government borrowing costs to their highest level in 24 years in a frantic day’s trading.
The threat of a renewed round of inflation from the persistently high cost of oil has spooked investors on both sides of the Atlantic, with central banks expected to raise interest rates in the coming months to prevent price increases from becoming embedded.
The sell-off drove the yield, or interest rate, on 10-year US Treasuries to 5.34% – the highest level since 2002.
In the UK, where surging borrowing costs are increasing the pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, before his first budget later this month, the yield on 30-year bonds hit 6% for the first time since 1998, before easing slightly later in the day. Yields on five- and 10-year UK bonds were also up.
Stock market investors sold heavily too, knocking almost 1.7% off the FTSE 100 in London – its worst daily fall since May. Bourses in other parts of Europe were also hit, with Germany’s DAX falling 1% and France’s CAC 40 losing 1.6%.
“There is carnage in the bond market, which is hitting stocks hard,” said Neil Wilson, the investor strategist at Saxo UK. “It looks like the relentless rout in the bond market is sending investors running for cover.”
The bond sell-off around the world is being driven by fears of high inflation, as the Middle East conflict continues to restrict oil supplies from the region.
Japan’s 10-year yield rose towards the 30-year high set last month.
US bonds weakened despite inflation data on Wednesday coming in lower than forecast, which was expected to calm investors’ nerves about the prospect of further increases in the cost of borrowing by the US Federal Reserve.
Traders remain anxious that the Fed will continue to raise interest rates to fight inflation, mainly in response to the strength of the US economy and the prospect of workers bidding up their wages.
Mohit Kumar, an economist at Jefferies, said there was growing concern at the amount of debt being issued to fund government deficits, as well as inflation concerns.
“Inflation, deficit and issuance concerns continue to weigh on the bond market,” he said.
“There is also a buyers’ strike as investors do not want to step in till we get some form of stability. Hedge funds have suffered in the latest round of sell-off and do not have the risk appetite to fade the move. Real money potentially has the risk appetite, but won’t step in till we get some stability.”
after newsletter promotion
Axel Rudolph, the chief technical analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “While the latest data has reduced expectations of an October Fed rate hike, investors remain wary that persistent inflation and higher oil prices could keep rates elevated for longer.
“The dollar is benefiting from that caution, climbing to a three-month high, while the prospect of a December rate increase keeps pressure on bond markets.”
Oil prices rose again on Thursday, despite analysis that showed exports of crude from the strait of Hormuz have largely returned to levels seen before the outbreak of the Iran war , as oil producers and the shipping industry have found alternative ways of transporting crucial fuel out of the Middle East.
Brent crude rose 3% to about $101 a barrel.
The price of crude remained at elevated levels as traders balanced the recovery in some Middle East exports with uncertainty over a long-term solution to the conflict and reopening of the strait.
Eurozone countries were also caught up in the wave of selling, with France in particular in investors’ sights. Ten-year yields on French government bonds hit 4.96%, the highest level since 2002.
The spread over German yields – an indicator of the additional risk France is believed to face – has jumped to its highest level in more than a decade.

articles.title_orig: A judge permanently dismisses former Olympian's Reflecting Pool charges
articles.title_zh: A judge permanently dismisses former Olympian's Reflecting Pool charges
articles.content_orig:
Former Olympic canoeist David Hearn, left, and his attorney Norm Eisen, right, leave D.C. court with a smile in early September after a hearing about the dismissal of his vandalism charges. Mark Schiefelbein/AP hide caption
A judge has dismissed with prejudice the government's vandalism charges against former Olympic canoeist David Hearn. That means federal prosecutors cannot refile them in the future, despite President Trump's public demands to do so.
In fact, as D.C. Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman explained in a 26-page ruling released Thursday, the case should be permanently closed in large part because of the "political pressure brought by the President of the United States upon his subordinate officers."
"While the prosecutors admit that the evidence indicates that he committed no crime, the President's statements create a risk that Mr. Hearn will be prosecuted nonetheless, either because the current United States Attorney and her assistants will eventually yield to his public pressure campaign or because the President will replace them with prosecutors more likely to carry out his wishes," wrote Edelman, an Obama appointee.
Hearn, 67, was arrested at the Reflecting Pool in June, around the time its multimillion-dollar new blue lining started noticeably peeling off in chunks. He was charged with one felony count of property destruction and quickly indicted by a grand jury , though he pleaded not guilty .
In late July, however, with a trial start date — and the prospect of up to 10 years in prison if convicted — looming, Pirro's office abruptly asked the judge to drop the charges against Hearn and three others altogether.
Citing new reports from the Department of the Interior and National Park Service, federal prosecutors admitted that the Reflecting Pool damage was, in fact, "the result of botched installation and not vandalism."
Trump disagreed, and publicly urged Pirro to revisit the case — which Thursday's ruling prevents.
When asked for comment, the White House referred NPR to three of Trump's Truth Social posts from August, blaming the Reflecting Pool damage on vandals and disagreeing with U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro's decision to drop charges against Hearn in the first place.
Hearn's supporters rally outside the District of Columbia Courthouse during an early September hearing. Mark Schiefelbein/AP hide caption
Neither the U.S. Attorney's Office for D.C. nor the Department of Justice returned NPR's requests for comment in time for publication.
Hearn's lawyers — Norm Eisen, Mary Dohrmann, Steve Levin and Michael Bromwich — celebrated the ruling in a joint statement, calling it "a victory for the rule of law and for an innocent American seeking justice."
"This case never should have been brought in the first place," they said. "This was a miscarriage of justice, and what happened to Mr. Hearn is an outrage that should shock every American."
The soft-spoken Maryland resident quickly became a cause célèbre for the many Americans captivated by the Reflecting Pool saga , which some saw as a referendum on the Trump administration itself.
In an August interview with NPR , Hearn described his experience as "Kafkaesque" and "Orwellian," but said he was buoyed by the support he'd received from within and beyond his community.
"With the power of the law, the power of the courts, and my wonderful team, I feel very well equipped … to bring democracy back to me," he said.
Trump railed against Pirro in the days and weeks after she dropped the charges, saying she had "choked" and "folded like an umbrella" — and didn't rule out firing her. He continued to blame the damage on vandalism and wrote on social media that anyone who disagreed "should go back to Law School."
"Most concerningly," Edelman wrote, during that time, the president also leveled increasingly personal attacks against Hearn and his legal team.
"U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro should re-visit her hastily made decision, especially since it turned out that the 'gentleman' involved is a big player in ActBlue, a disgraceful fundraising SCAM, and is represented by a TRUMP DERANGED SLEAZEBAG, Political Hack Lawyer, Norm Eisen," Trump wrote in early August , in one of the social media posts the White House directed NPR to on Thursday.
It's against that backdrop that Hearn's legal team has been lobbying the judge to dismiss the charges with prejudice, to prevent the same case from being revived. The Trump administration, on the other hand, sought to leave that door open.
Edelman's Thursday ruling offers a peek into the government's argument — and then dismantles it.
The empty, fenced-off Reflecting Pool as seen in late September. Rod Lamkey/AP hide caption
Edelman wrote that when asked in court what kind of hypothetical new evidence might prompt prosecutors to revisit the case, an unnamed assistant U.S. attorney "waxed philosophical, musing, 'I don't know what the future may bring. None of us do.'"
He says prosecutors could not provide any specific examples of such evidence, and "admitted that the government was no longer even investigating the case."
"Given its own description of the existing evidence and the circumstances of this case, the development of contrary evidence seems practically inconceivable, and the possibility of a future meritorious prosecution strikes the Court as fanciful," Edelman concluded.
Hearn's lawyers say Thursday's ruling allows him "to move forward with his life as he deserves."
The Reflecting Pool, which was drained after July 4th, remains empty and fenced off for repairs, with no public timeline for completion.

articles.content_orig:
Vladimir Putin has said Russia will use all weapons at his disposal if it considers its Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad to have come under direct attack.
The Russian president insisted that Moscow was "not threatening anyone" and merely responding to statements by Western leaders that it was preparing for war in 2029 or 2030.
Throughout this week, Russia has accused Nato of preparing to blockade its territory, which borders Lithuania and Poland, warning that it would even be prepared to use nuclear weapons if the West tried to cut off Kaliningrad from the rest of Russia.
Nato has sought to calm the situation, stressing that it was a defensive alliance and urging Moscow to stop its "nuclear threats".
Western allies have faced a surge in so-called hybrid warfare incidents blamed on Russia, particularly in Poland and the Baltics in recent months.
Last week alone, Poland said a Russian helicopter had strayed into its territory adjacent to Kaliningrad and Lithuania said its population felt "constantly threatened" by Russia, in part because of drones entering the nation's airspace.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Thursday that his country was preparing for further hybrid attacks, "including serious ones", after a drone armed with explosives was found in August on the tarmac at Leipzig airport close to Ukrainian cargo planes.
Rosenberg: Putin shows no sign of stopping the war as Russia doubles down on Ukraine
In a wide-ranging speech at the Valdai foreign policy forum, Putin told his audience that he believed that international conflicts were highly likely to continue, but would get better as "Western hegemony" weakened.
Although the Russian leader himself began the full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022, he again blamed the West for provoking the invasion, arguing that Moscow had simply been forced to defend itself and take up arms.
He also insisted that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian economic targets were a direct response to Ukraine's strikes on Russia's oil refineries and its ships in the Black Sea.
"Now from every direction we're receiving calls 'let's stop'. But they started it," he said.
Putin admitted Kyiv had "got some results" from its refinery attacks and Russia had lost about 1% of its GDP. Ukraine maintains it began attacking Russian oil infrastructure because it helped the Kremlin finance the war.
Russia has targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, ramping up attacks every winter since the war in Ukraine started in 2022. Other civilian infrastructure is also regularly hit, with a key bridge in Kyiv attacked by drones on Thursday.
Putin also accused the West of instigating other conflicts.
"If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation, in this case we are talking about Kaliningrad but possibly some other territories, of course the issue of use by the Russian Federation of all arms at the disposal of our country will inevitably and immediately be on the agenda," he said.
He accused Nato of holding naval manoeuvres in the Baltic Sea that he argued represented serious threats to Kaliningrad. If the territory came under Western blockade, he said Russia would be prepared to use all means and forces, including nuclear.
"We are not threatening anyone. We do not intend to attack anyone in 2029, in 2030, in 2050. But if we come across an aggression we will have to respond. Citizens of European countries should be fully aware of that."
He added that while he was aware of the nuclear capabilities of countries such as the UK and France, the weapons at its disposal were unparalleled.
Western officials have long feared that, rather than invading Kaliningrad, Russia would use the relatively small distance between the exclave and ally Belarus - known as the Suwalki Gap - were it to attempt to seize Lithuanian territory by force.
Lithuania's prime minister told the BBC last week that his country had made evacuation plans in case Russia invaded and thousands of Nato troops are stationed there.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte made clear on Wednesday that none of the alliance's "exercises or activities" posed any threat to Moscow and that the Kremlin's messaging was "absolutely not called for and not helpful".
Putin spent some time talking about leading countries in the world having armaments at their disposal that could "swipe away all life or at least push the Earth to catastrophic consequences", and said that unfortunately no-one could be sure they would never be used.
He drew the analogy of a gun sitting on a theatre stage - if it was hanging there at the start of the show, it would certainly be fired at the end.
He appeared to call for the rules of warfare to be rewritten and warned of the increasing risk of artificial intelligence.
"The automation and digitalisation of warfare leads to its gamification. This leads to degradation and sliding back of humanity to barbarity," he said.

articles.title_orig: Cornell Jane Doe's attorney says she told police in 2024: 'I was raped'
articles.title_zh: Cornell Jane Doe's attorney says she told police in 2024: 'I was raped'
articles.content_orig:
Students walk on the campus of Cornell University on Wednesday in Ithaca, N.Y. Spencer Platt/Getty Images hide caption
The woman who alleges she was gang raped by fellow Cornell University students in 2024 clearly stated in her statement to police two years ago that she was sexually assaulted.
That's according to her attorney, Thomas Giuffra, who confirmed to NPR that his client told investigators, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped," citing transcripts from Jane Doe's sworn statement in 2024.
NPR asked Giuffra to specifically confirm on the record to NPR that his client made this exact quoted statement regarding her assault. His response by text: "Yes she did."
This is in contrast to statements from the local prosecutor, who claimed on Monday that Doe never stated she was raped. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten told NPR local station WSKG on Wednesday that he had not read the full account of her detailed statements to investigators where she repeatedly described being assaulted.
NPR asked Cornell if campus police provided the DA with all of the information from their investigation, including her repeated statements about being assaulted. The university did not respond to the request for comment.
CBS News New York reported Wednesday on a transcript of an interview between the Cornell University Police Department investigator and the alleged victim. NPR has not been able to obtain a copy of these transcripts.
Van Houten said in Monday's statement that in the 2024 statement taken by Cornell University police, Doe "did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped. On the contrary, Jane Doe's statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual."
No criminal charges were ever filed against the seven men Doe alleges drugged and assaulted her for several hours in October 2024.
Van Houten told NPR member station WSKG on Wednesday evening that he was in the process of getting the interview transcript from Cornell. He told the station over email that he doesn't know when he will get the transcript from the university "or if Cornell will resist turning it over."
"If it's factual, we absolutely should have been informed about what Jane Doe said to police that was not in her six-page statement," he told WSKG.
Van Houten said earlier this week that his office is reexamining the case.
He added that particular transcript is part of the confidential Title IX investigation Cornell launched into the alleged assault.
In mid-September, Doe filed a lawsuit against the seven men who she alleges assaulted her two years ago. Cornell was also named in the lawsuit.
Following the onslaught of public backlash against Cornell and the local prosecutor, the school said Wednesday night that it will bring in an outside counsel to conduct an independent probe into the handling of the case.
Since Tuesday, Cornell has directed the public to an FAQ page on the rape allegations.
The university has maintained that Cornell University Police investigated the case thoroughly and that the school held its own Title IX investigation, which resulted in suspensions and expulsions. Cornell has not specified how many students faced punishments, or of what nature. It noted in the FAQ: "Federal privacy law prohibits Cornell from disclosing specific information regarding individual students, and the university is therefore unable to make a public statement regarding any other disciplinary response."
WSKG found that as of Wednesday, the university has changed its FAQ. And it has quietly removed a sentence stating that the Cornell police "shared all investigatory information with the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office."
Previously, the FAQ read: "The Cornell University Police Department investigated the matter in 2024 and shared all investigatory information with the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office, which is the established protocol if the department believes it is possible a crime has occurred."
But by Wednesday afternoon , WSKG found that statement had been edited, and any mention of Cornell police sharing "all investigatory information" with the district attorney had disappeared from the page.
"The Cornell University Police Department is a unit of the university, and its officers are sworn Tompkins County deputy sheriffs whose duties include the enforcement of law and order on Cornell property," the new statement reads. "This incident occurred in Cornell's jurisdiction."
WSKG reported that Cornell University did not respond to its questions about these changes.
Students at the university have expressed outrage and deep disappointment toward school officials for their handling of this case. The Cornell University Student Assembly scheduled a public hearing set for Thursday afternoon during which they say they will "demand institutional accountability" from their school.
"We stand unequivocally with survivors of sexual violence, and we remain committed to ensuring that their voices are not only heard, but met with action," the organization said in a statement on Instagram .
Late Wednesday, the school confirmed to NPR that it is bringing in an outside counsel to hold an independent examination of the alleged gang rape.
University officials told NPR they have no further details about how the investigation will play out. Previously, Cornell strongly defended how it handled the case when Doe first reported the incident to school officials two years ago.
The move comes after New York Gov. Kathy Hochul called for the school to open an outside investigation. In a video posted on X , Hochul also said she's considering new legislation to tighten sexual assault laws across the state.
"While we have some of the toughest laws on sexual assault on college campuses right here in New York, I think we can do better," she said. "This culture has to stop. And it will stop here in the state of New York."
WSKG's Aurora Berry contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Renee Good's family sues Trump administration over fatal Minneapolis shooting
articles.title_zh: Renee Good's family sues Trump administration over fatal Minneapolis shooting
articles.content_orig:
The family of Renee Good, one of two US citizens fatally shot by federal immigration agents in the state of Minnesota, has sued the government over her killing during a sweeping immigrant deportation blitz in January.
The two lawsuits – filed on Thursday by Good’s partner, Becca Good, and Renee’s brother, Brent Ganger – say officials from US President Donald Trump’s administration were reckless and violated the civil rights of Good and others in Minneapolis. The lawsuits are demanding a jury trial and financial damages.
The lawsuits are the first major civil actions taken against the Trump administration over its unprecedented deportation crackdowns in Minneapolis last winter, dubbed Operation Metro Surge.
The first lawsuit seeks damages for Good’s wrongful death under Minnesota law, citing claims of assault, battery, false imprisonment, negligence and intentional infliction of emotional distress.
The second lawsuit alleges a civil rights conspiracy among numerous defendants including the immigration officer and shooter Jonathon Ross, who was named alongside high-ranking Trump administration officials, including White House Deputy Policy Chief Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, former Border Patrol commander Gregory Bovino and Trump’s longtime campaign adviser, Corey Lewandowski.
Good, a mother of three, was shot and killed in her car by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent in south Minneapolis when she and her wife joined one of the city’s daily demonstrations against masked and armed federal agents deployed to the city to arrest migrants for deportation.
Widespread cellphone footage taken by eyewitnesses captured the moment in which Good was killed, after agent Ross fired into the windshield, shooting her in the head, arm and torso.
Federal officials at the time said the officer acted in self-defence and that Good had engaged in “an act of domestic terrorism”.
In a statement posted on Truth Social at the time, Trump defended the deadly ICE shooting, saying that the reason those “incidents” were happening was that “the Radical Left is threatening, assaulting, and targeting our Law Enforcement Officers and ICE Agents on a daily basis”.
Days after the shooting, officials from the US Department of Justice, including then-Deputy Attorney Todd Blanche, blocked federal prosecutors from pursuing a criminal civil rights case against the agents involved in her killing, which prompted at least half a dozen of those prosecutors to resign in protest.
Minnesota sued the Trump administration in March to gain access to the evidence it gathered at the shooting scenes, but investigations stalled after the Justice Department halted its routine cooperation and evidence-sharing with the Minneapolis Police Department.
None of the agents involved in Good’s killing has faced any charges.

articles.title_orig: Former Dallas officer convicted of killing Black man in his apartment granted parole
articles.title_zh: Former Dallas officer convicted of killing Black man in his apartment granted parole
articles.content_orig:
A former Dallas police officer was granted parole on Thursday just under seven years after she was convicted of murdering her neighbor in a 2018 shooting.
Amber Guyger , 38, was granted parole by the Texas Board of Pardons and Paroles, the board said in a statement. In 2019, Guyger was convicted of murdering 26-year-old Black man Botham Jean.
Guyger told authorities that she shot Jean after mistakenly walking into his apartment, believing it to be her own, according to officials. She told authorities she believed Jean was an intruder. Jean was eating ice cream in his living room and not armed, according to authorities.
The former police officer was sentenced to 10 years in prison for the crime. Prosecutors asked jurors to sentence Guyger to at least 28 years.
The Texas board said that Guyger was granted parole because she did not have a documented pattern of violent arrests, she “maintained a satisfactory institutional adjustment” and completed programs “that should enhance chances to obtain and maintain full-time stable employment” during her imprisonment.
Guyger initially became eligible for parole on September 29, 2024. Her initial review occurred on October 10, 2024, and resulted in a parole denial with her next review being scheduled on or about October 2026.
During her trial, questions were raised about the role race may have played in the killing.
Prosecutors revealed racist text messages the former police officer sent, unrelated to Jean or his killing.
One of the texts was about the Martin Luther King Jr. parade in Dallas in 2018.
“When does this end lol,” an officer wrote to Guyger.
“When MLK is dead … oh wait …,” she joked.
Two days before Guyger killed Jean, she texted someone who had just adopted a German Shepherd.
The dog’s owner wrote that the dog “may be racist.”
Guyger replied: “It’s okay ... I’m the same.”
Prosecutors said that Jean was watching television and eating a bowl of vanilla ice cream in his living room just before 10 p.m. when Guyger burst inside and shot him.
Guyger testified that she used her electronic key fob to open Jean’s door and that she immediately drew her service weapon once she was inside.
The prosecution said the trajectory of the bullet showed that Jean was either getting up from his couch or cowering when Guyger fired at him.
A lawyer for Jean’s family, Lee Merritt, said in a statement to NBC News Dallas-Fort Worth that the family was “disappointed by the decision.”
“A 10-year sentence was already a fraction of what was lost,” Merritt said. “Releasing Ms. Guyger after seven years makes that loss feel even smaller in the eyes of the system. It is not. The family still lives with this loss every day.”
Jean’s family said in a statement on Thursday that they are requesting privacy at this time.
“To all of the many well-wishers who have continued to say Botham’s name and carry his memory, they wish to give their thanks for the continuing support,” the family said in a statement.
Jean’s brother, Brandt Jean, said he forgave Guyger during her sentencing in 2019.
“I personally want the best for you,” he said at the time. “I wasn’t even going to say this before my family, but I don’t even want you to go to jail. I want the best for you, because I know that’s exactly what Botham would want you to do — to give your life to Christ.”
The Dallas Police Department said in a statement that it had “no role in this decision.”
“The Dallas Police Department understands this decision may bring renewed attention and emotion surrounding the tragic death of Botham Jean,” the department said. “Our thoughts remain with the Jean family and all those impacted by his loss.”
Jean grew up in Saint Lucia before coming to the United States to go to Harding University in Arkansas, which he graduated from in 2016. He was working as an accountant for one of the most prestigious accounting firms in the world, PricewaterhouseCoopers, in Dallas when he was killed.
He would have turned 35-years-old on Tuesday.
I’m a reporter on NBC News’ breaking news team, covering crime, extreme weather, pop culture and more. I recently covered Hurricane Milton, which devastated the Tampa, Florida, metropolitan area, and the student-led protests at Columbia University.

articles.title_zh: Netanyahu: Omani co-pilot went through Islamic radicalization
articles.content_orig:
Alleged flydubai attacker interrogated by Saudi security services as investigation into apparent crash attempt opens
The Omani co-pilot who stabbed his captain in an apparent attempt to crash an Israel-bound flight from Dubai had previously undergone radical Islamist indoctrination and was suicidal, Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu , has claimed.
Israeli passengers intervened to stop the attack on Wednesday, restraining the co-pilot, while a reserve crew in the plane was able to stabilise the plummeting plane and ultimately land it safely in Saudi Arabia.
The plane had more than 170 people onboard and Israeli officials praised the bravery of those who intervened, announcing that four of the Israeli passengers would receive a “heroism” award for preventing a potential disaster.
Netanyahu told Fox News: “We know that he underwent Islamic radical indoctrination. That appears to be something we are gathering from his personal information.”
The co-pilot, whose identity is still not known, was being interrogated by Saudi security services, which arrested him on the plane’s arrival in Tabuk, in the north-west of the country.
Saudi investigators were cooperating with the United Arab Emirates , the US, Oman and Israel to try to determine the attacker’s motive, a regional official familiar with the investigation said. “All possible scenarios, from terrorism to mental disorders, are being looked into. Nothing is ruled out for now,” they told the Associated Press.
Two Israeli security officials said that Israel’s initial assessment was that the co-pilot was probably acting alone, Reuters reported.
Netanyahu said that the co-pilot was probably suicidal, citing preliminary “indications”.
“It looks very likely that he was going to down the plane … The Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that are found in his background, I think that’s a pretty good clue,” he said, emphasising that final conclusions had yet to be made.
Netanyahu had previously said it was “too early to say” if there was any state backing – namely Iranian – of the attack. Two Israeli security sources told Reuters that they had not yet found Iranian involvement.
The attack came just days after Netanyahu warned of an unspecified security threat to Israel that could come during its October election. The Israeli military had said before the incident it had no specific intelligence of an imminent threat and the opposition leader Yair Lapid said that a security briefing on Tuesday night included no mention of a related threat.
Other Israeli officials, including the defence minister, Israel Katz, and the ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, suggested the incident was a “terror attack”, with the Israeli foreign ministry briefing its diplomats that the attack was against Israel and its relationship with the UAE.
Donald Trump suggested the co-pilot was “perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack job”, and told reporters at the White House that he and Netanyahu had spoken at length.
Netanyahu also spoke to the president of the UAE, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, who agreed to Israel’s involvement in the investigation.
Flydubai said its flights to and from Israel would be suspended while the investigation took place and urged all parties “to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts”.
The UAE announced on Thursday that it would conduct its own investigation into the incident, which started about two and a half hours after takeoff from Dubai. It said its investigators had begun to look into the attacker’s motive and if he had any links to any “terrorist purpose”.
Passengers said they saw a knife-wielding man – apparently the Omani co-pilot – putting the captain of the plane on the floor, after which the plane began to plummet. The wounded pilot, Smit Machchhar, an Indian national, managed to send out an emergency signal and open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter and stop the plane’s descent.
A video shared by the prime minister’s office showed one passenger, Yaniv Hayoun, a plumber, speaking to Netanyahu at length about how the events onboard had played out.
Hayoun told the prime minister he and other passengers heard screaming and felt the air pressure change as the plane dived before they forced their way into the cockpit and found the attacker at the instrument panel. “I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and dragged him out first,” Hayoun said during the meeting with Netanyahu after the plane had landed safely and the passengers were flown to Israel.
Machchhar was widely praised for his bravery, with Netanyahu and the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, hailing him as a hero. India’s ambassador to the UAE met the wounded captain’s family and briefed them on his recovery, the Indian consulate in the UAE said.
Machchhar was being treated in a hospital in Tabuk , but was in good health and recovering well, according to the Indian embassy in the UAE, which said the ambassador had visited the pilot.
“Captain Smit Machchhar is a HERO,” Modi said, in a post on social media. “In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others.”

articles.title_zh: ‘Fatal point of no return’: Putin warns against use of nukes amid global tensions
articles.content_orig:
Vladimir Putin has said Russia will use all weapons at his disposal if it considers it has come under direct attack in its Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad.
Addressing the Valdai foreign policy forum, Putin insisted Russia was "not threatening anyone" and merely responding to statements by Western leaders that Moscow was preparing for war in 2029 or 2030.
Throughout this week, Russia has accused Nato of preparing to blockade its territory, which borders Lithuania and Poland, warning that it would even be prepared to use nuclear weapons if the West tried to cut off Kaliningrad from the rest of Russia.
Nato has sought to calm the situation, stressing it is a defensive alliance and urging Moscow to stop its "nuclear threats".
Western allies have faced a surge in so-called hybrid warfare incidents blamed on Russia, particularly in Poland and the Baltics in recent months.
Last week alone Poland said a Russian helicopter had strayed into its territory adjacent to Kaliningrad and Lithuania said its population felt "constantly threatened" by Russia, in part because of drones entering the nation's airspace.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Thursday that his country was preparing for further hybrid attacks, "including serious ones", after a drone armed with explosives was found in August on the tarmac at Leipzig airport close to Ukrainian cargo planes.
Rosenberg: Putin shows no sign of stopping the war as Russia doubles down on Ukraine
In a wide-ranging speech, the Russian leader told his audience he believed that international conflicts were highly likely to continue, but would get better as "Western hegemony" weakened.
Although Putin himself began the full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022, he again blamed the West for provoking the invasion, arguing that it had simply been forced to defend itself and take up arms.
He also insisted that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian economic targets were a direct response to Ukraine's strikes on Russia's oil refineries, and on its ships in the Black Sea.
"Now from every direction we're receiving calls 'let's stop'. But they started it," he said.
Putin admitted Kyiv had "got some results" from its refinery attacks and Russia had lost about 1% of its GDP. Ukraine maintains it began attacking Russian oil infrastructure because it helped the Kremlin finance the war.
Russia has targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, ramping up attacks every winter since the war on Ukraine started in 2022. Other civilian infrastructure is also regularly hit, and a key bridge in Kyiv was attacked by drones on Thursday.
Putin also accused the West of instigating other conflicts.
"If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation, in this case we are talking about Kaliningrad but possibly some other territories, of course the issue of use by the Russian Federation of all arms at the disposal of our country will inevitably and immediately be on the agenda," he said.
He accused Nato of holding naval manoeuvres in the Baltic Sea which he argued represented serious threats to Kaliningrad. If the territory came under Western blockade, he said Russia would be prepared to use all means and forces, including nuclear.
"We are not threatening anyone. We do not intend to attack anyone in 2029, in 2030, in 2050. But if we come across an aggression we will have to respond. Citizens of European countries should be fully aware of that."
He added that while he was aware of the nuclear capabilities of countries such as the UK and France, the weapons at its disposal were unparalleled.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte made clear on Wednesday that none of the alliance's "exercises or activities" posed any threat to Moscow and the Kremlin's messaging was "absolutely not called for and not helpful".
Putin spent some time talking about leading countries in the world having armaments at their disposal that could "swipe away all life or at least push the Earth to catastrophic consequences", and said unfortunately no-one could be sure they would never be used.
He drew the analogy of a gun sitting on a theatre stage - if it was hanging there at the start of the show, it would certainly fire at the end.
He appeared to call for the rules of warfare to be rewritten, and warned of the increasing risk of artificial intelligence.
"The automation and digitalisation of warfare leads to its gamification. This leads to degradation and sliding back of humanity to barbarity," he said.

WASHINGTON — President Trump on Monday headed into a week full of high-stakes meetings with world leaders after spending a 72-hour period banning reporters from the White House, mulling whether it was time to “blow ... up” Iran, and proposing to host military drones and snipers  at his triumphal arch in the nation’s capital.
The weekend — which also included the announcement of a security deal over Greenland and the creation of a new “A.I. Force” — captured an American president operating unpredictably across multiple fronts even as each one drew friction. The actions now stand to color the backdrop of a week that will feature meetings with world leaders at the United Nations General Assembly in New York and a state visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington.
Each of those moves carries its own political weight ahead of the diplomatic talks, but also ahead of the midterm elections, where these topics are front and center in key races.
Trump’s handling of the Iran war, its subsequent shocks to the global economy, his push to fast-track the development of artificial intelligence and the Greenland agreement are likely to come up in meetings with world leaders. His deal with Denmark to bolster U.S. military presence in Greenland, a territory Trump has repeatedly tried to annex , is expected to be signed  Tuesday in New York, though action is still needed by the Danish and Greenland governments before it can be enforced.
While all the details of the Greenland deal are not public yet, Trump has said it is a “dream come true for the United States of America.”
“This solution is a great one for the United States of America, Denmark, Greenland and all of our Allies,” Trump wrote on social media Friday. “We look forward to working with the wonderful people of Denmark and Greenland toward a magnificent future with respect to this large, and highly strategic, parcel of land. We will be very protective of it.”
In an interview  Sunday, Trump also indicated that he was trying to make a decision on Iran as the war stretches into its eighth month. The president said he would “probably be open” to meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian during the U.N. General Assembly.
“My question is, if and when do I blow the entire nation up?” Trump told Fox News. “They better behave.”
CNN, MS NOW and Politico will challenge the constitutionality of President Trump’s order to ban the news organizations from the White House.
Of all the actions Trump took, the press dispute has become the most contentious and drawn an immediate legal response. Three major news outlets — CNN, MS NOW and Politico — sued the Trump administration Monday for banning their reporters from the White House grounds, and major television networks suspended their pool coverage of the president’s activities.
In a joint statement, the organizations said the White House has acted “without notice or process” and called the arbitrary decision a “blatant violation” of the 1st Amendment.
Trump, meanwhile, argued  Monday that the banned  news outlets  are “corrupt” and a “threat to our national security.”
Vice President JD Vance defended the press ban.
“He’s not banning media outlets. What he’s doing is saying we’re not going to give you special access to the White House if you engage in what is effectively propaganda,” Vance said Monday, arguing that the three outlets push out “negative” coverage of Trump.
The tense showdown between Trump and the White House press corps led to audio problems during the president’s ribbon-cutting ceremony for a new helipad on the South Lawn. Without television cameras and microphones set up by the major TV networks, it was impossible to hear what  Trump was saying through the White House’s official YouTube stream, signaling  further technical difficulties in the week ahead.
Behind the public displays of control, news reports have painted a picture of a president increasingly frustrated by the lack of credit he feels he is owed. At a recent closed-door meeting, reported by the Wall Street Journal , Trump told advisors he was aggravated that his allies hadn’t lauded him enough for his efforts to take over the Kennedy Center or other accomplishments made during his second term.
Trump has tried to put his name on the building’s facade and run into resistance from Democrats, arts patrons and a federal judge who blocked the move last week. Trump was then photographed aboard Air Force One looking at a large printout appearing to show demolition plans for the center.
Ahead of the meeting, rhetoric from Washington and Beijing has underscored only deepening acrimony and distrust over their rush to dominate the technological frontier.
Over the weekend, Trump posted on social media a link to a news article that claimed he was seeking to fix “safety hazards” at the performance center. He then posted an image of him watching the  Western Hemisphere with the words, “His Hemisphere,” and wrote that his proposed triumphal arch near the National Mall would be used as a military complex for drones and snipers.
Trump also announced that he would be creating the “A.I. force,” modeled after the Space Force he launched during his first term, to ensure the country does not “in any way hinder or stifle the growth of the industry.” The announcement came amid growing backlash to data centers and the fast-paced development of artificial intelligence, an issue that in recent weeks has prompted stark warnings about the technology’s power and its threats to humanity.
Tech executives, including Dario Amodei and Sam Altman, have even called for a slowdown on the technology’s advancement and last week, four leading AI companies — Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Google — faced a lawsuit claiming they made an illegal deal to slow the pace of their respective AI development.
Trump’s announcement over the weekend comes as lawmakers, including congressional Republicans in tight  races, have called for new guardrails on the technology.
Despite technology becoming a political flashpoint during the midterms, Trump has dismissed concerns about AI as a hoax and asserted that those who oppose data centers are intent on being “backwards and poor.”
Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) is among the lawmakers who have called for action on regulating the technology, and he has warned that not doing so could come at a cost on Nov. 3.
“We really need to send a memo around explaining we’ve got midterm elections coming,” Kennedy told Politico. “I may send that out.”

NFL.com editors Jeremy Bergman , Brooke Cersosimo , Gennaro Filice , Bobby Kownack and Dan Parr will predict the winner of every game in the 2026 NFL season, using the unbeatable combo of football analysis and excessive punctuation. Check out their Week 4 NFL picks below.
Why Dan picked the Steelers: I know the recent history of the Steelers’ trips to Cleveland -- it’s the stuff of nightmares for Pittsburgh -- but I’m not ready to trust the Browns’ offense. It ranks among the bottom-five units in too many categories, including total yards, third-down conversion rate and red zone touchdown percentage. Now, I’m certainly not convinced the Steelers are a finely-tuned offensive machine, either, even after their 30-point outburst against the Bengals . Mike McCarthy’s crew was held to three points in a loss less than two weeks ago, so I’m predicting a low-scoring contest on Thursday night. If the Browns’ defense -- led by second-year breakout DT Mason Graham -- keeps Aaron Rodgers from ever getting comfortable, the upset will be in play. I saw too many poor throws from Deshaun Watson last week to forecast such an outcome, though, especially with injuries leaving Cleveland vulnerable on the interior of the offensive line .
Why Jeremy picked the Commanders: With or without Jayden Daniels , Washington has a chance to give the Colts fits in London. Jonathan Taylor , Indy's main outlet for offensive production over the years, is facing a Commanders run defense that ranks third in the NFL through three weeks. Taylor is an international legend after last year's blistering Berlin showing , but he hasn't broken 100 yards in a game this season. Washington has been careful with the ball on offense, committing just one giveaway all year, while the Colts defense has been among the league's worst in terms of yards and points allowed but also takeaways (1). Both clubs are turning a corner after getting off the schneid in Week 3, but the Commanders are in a better place, even with their starting quarterback rehabbing another dislocated elbow.
Why Jeremy picked the Ravens: Derrick Henry 's first meeting with his former team isn't necessarily a "revenge game." After all, he left the Titans in 2024 as they downsized, and little of the regime that "shipped" him out remains. That fact won't stop Henry from trying to run all over Tennessee on Sunday afternoon. History, however, may be against Henry; no player has ever rushed for at least 100 yards against a team with which he recorded at least 9,000 career rushing yards. Plus, the Titans, for all their faults in this season's early going, have been competitive against the run, allowing just 3.6 yards per attempt. When Henry plows into the teeth of the Titans front on Sunday, Jeffery Simmons has vowed to "hit his ass." Tennessee's main issue remains Cam Ward , the offense and its slow starts. The Titans should expect no relief against a Ravens outfit rejuvenated by its resounding win in Rio .
Why Gennaro picked the Bills: What is the best representation of New England’s well-documented offensive struggles? I’m partial to one simple statistic that has made the rounds this week: In 30 offensive drives this season, the Patriots have scored 29 points. For comparison’s sake, the Bills have logged 32 offensive drives … and scored 101 points. Another painful Pats stat that’s burning up the interwebs: Going back to January’s playoffs, Drake Maye has turned the ball over 15 times in his past seven games. What on earth has happened to last season’s MVP runner-up? The 24-year-old’s putrid play has spawned theories far and wide, some more conspiratorial than others. Is Cover 6 his kryptonite? Is the shoulder still barking from last season’s injury? Is there a rift between Maye and Mike Vrabel? I won’t pretend to have any of those answers, but one thing is pretty easy to surmise: The quarterback misses A.J. Brown . Unfortunately, the blockbuster trade acquisition’s high ankle sprain is expected to keep him out until late October . And in the here and now, New England’s other notable offseason addition out wide, Romeo Doubs , has gotten off to a rough start in Foxborough. If Maye and Co. are indeed suffering the infamous Super Bowl hangover, it’s hard to believe the best remedy is a trip to Buffalo for a game against their undefeated division rivals.
NFL media analyst Brett Kollmann comments on quarterback Drake Maye and the New England Patriots so far this season.
Why Brooke picked the Bears: Will the Bears start Case Keenum or Tyson Bagent at quarterback? That's the question Ben Johnson must weigh. The veteran diced up the Eagles on Monday night , but the HC insists there are reasons Bagent ended camp as QB2 . We'll find out soon enough, but no matter. The Jets have held a lead or been tied in the fourth quarter of all three games, but I don't see that to be the case Sunday after myriad injuries to key Jets, including RB Breece Hall , WR Adonai Mitchell , TE Mason Taylor , OG Dylan Parham ( all are week to week , per HC Aaron Glenn). The offense faces an uphill climb -- especially with its bell-cow back sidelined -- against a Bears D that has held its last two opponents to fewer than 10 points. New York's defense has impressed and made plays, to be sure. It's good enough to make stops, but can it make enough stops to help its undermanned offense keep pace? A competitive game gets away from Gang Green late with the league's top-ranked rushing attack running out the clock to give Chicago its second straight win at Soldier Field.
Why Bobby picked the Jaguars: After two superb weeks for Cincy’s defense, Bengals fans must have been having flashbacks to recent seasons as their team was suddenly unable to slow down the Steelers. Aaron Rodgers threw for over 290 yards and three touchdowns for the first time since he was a Packer in 2021, and Jaylen Warren went off for 176 yards from scrimmage. It’s just one game, but the result also necessitates looking back at the first two weeks that caused Cincinnati to earn praise for a supposed offseason transformation. The four takeaways against Tampa Bay in Week 1 were great, but the Bengals still gave up points to an offense that has since struggled. And after doing nothing against Cincinnati in Week 2, Houston was just quieted by a Colts team that had allowed the second-most yards through the first two games in a season in NFL history. Now the Jaguars come to town with the most high-functioning offense the Bengals have faced thus far -- by a wide margin. They just blew the doors off the reigning AFC champions, defeating the Patriots, 35-6 . Trevor Lawrence enters the contest playing well, with 616 passing yards, seven touchdowns, two picks and a 107.8 passer rating. If the Bengals prove unable to limit the damage again defensively, Joe Burrow and Co. will have a mighty tough task keeping up against the No. 1 defense in points allowed.

And he's yet face a DeMeco Ryans-led unit (with Houston or San Francisco), so things could continue to go south. The 25-year-old man is a dual British-Iranian citizen, authorities said in an update .
Police have also carried out searches of two properties in the Gloucestershire, England, area where the RAF base is located.
"The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of enquiry," said Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing.
"As we've made clear, we're looking at all possible angles -- including possible foreign state involvement."
Police initially reported that the man was 27 , but later corrected his age.
The other five men arrested in connection with the incident earlier this week have been released on bail.
On Wednesday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced that the incident was a foiled plot whose perpetrators are believed to have ties to Iran.
"There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford," he told the BBC .
Police found no explosive devices in three vans that were stopped near the base, which is used by the U.S. military to launch airstrikes on Iran, but gasoline was found.

Rapper Rick Ross was arrested Thursday after he was accused of beating his girlfriend at his Miami Beach home, according to authorities.
Ross, whose legal name is William Leonard Roberts II, was charged with felony battery by strangulation and misdemeanor battery in connection with a domestic violence incident at his home on Miami Beach’s exclusive Star Island, according to a statement and affidavit from the Miami Beach Police Department.
Police said the accuser reported that Ross, 50, struck her multiple times during an altercation on Aug. 28 and restricted her breathing by twisting the collar of her hoodie.
The woman, whom police did not name, reported the incident to police on Tuesday. Ross turned himself in Thursday morning. He has pleaded not guilty to the charges.
An attorney for Ross did not immediately return a request for comment.
The woman provided detectives with a sworn statement and photographs documenting her injuries, police said. A criminal affidavit identifies the woman as Ross’ girlfriend at the time of the incident.
On the morning of Aug. 28, Ross was “enraged” that his girlfriend was tagged in an Instagram photo, accused her of lying to him and slapped her across the face, the affidavit says.
Later that morning, according to the police record, Ross accused her of having a romantic relationship with someone she said she was “merely friends with.”
The woman told police that Ross then struck her in the chest several times and choked her “to the point she could not breathe by grabbing the collar of the hoodie she was wearing and twisting it,” the affidavit said.
Ross then grabbed her by her ponytail and slammed her against a wall, the affidavit says.
She told police she escaped the residence, returned and waited until Ross left before retrieving her belongings, according to the affidavit. The two dated for about a year, and lived together at the Star Island home at the time of the incident, the affidavit says.
Ross is best known for his breakout single “Hustlin’,” released in 2006, as well as “Aston Martin Music” and “Stay Schemin.” He’s received nine Grammy nominations.
The rapper’s bond was set at $5,000 for the battery by strangulation charge and $1,000 for the battery charge, according to online jail records.
“I’m totally innocent of these fabricated allegations made against me,” Ross said, leaving the jailhouse “I repeat: I’m totally innocent of these fabricated allegations made against me.”
Ross said he would be traveling to Dubai on Friday and in Paris on Saturday.
If you or someone you know is facing domestic violence, call the National Domestic Violence hotline for help at (800) 799-SAFE (7233), or go to www.thehotline.org for more. States often have domestic violence hotlines as well.
